You use the subjunctive after verbs of emotion (sono contento che, ho paura che, mi dispiace che) and after conjunctions (benché, affinché, prima che, a condizione che, senza che).
I'm afraid she won't like Naples.
Although she doesn't speak Italian, she makes herself understood very well.
I'll give you the recipe so you can make it at home.
I must leave before it gets dark.
To use the subjunctive after joy: sono contento / felice che.
To use the subjunctive after fear and worry: ho paura che, temo che.
To use the subjunctive after regret and surprise: mi dispiace che, è strano che.
To use the conjunctions that take the subjunctive: benché, affinché, prima che, a condizione che, purché, senza che.
To tell "perché + indicative" (because) apart from "perché + subjunctive" (so that).
To use the infinitive when the subject is the same: prima di partire, senza parlare.

The end of March, in Sibiu. Doina is going to spend Easter in Naples with Giulia's family, as Grandma Assunta wished. Ilinca will go with her. On the evening before they leave, everyone is in the kitchen.
I'm so glad your mother is going to Naples! Grandma has talked about nothing else for weeks.
Me too. But I'm a bit afraid she'll feel lost. She's never flown on her own.
She won't be alone: I'm going. And I've taken four days off so nobody worries.
Even though she doesn't speak Italian, you'll see she'll make herself understood. In Naples people talk with their hands!
I'm sorry we can't go. But with the work at the museum…
It's a pity, yes. But it's better for the two mothers to meet without us being there translating every word.
Giulia, what should Mum take? I'm afraid she'll take too much stuff.
The sarmale, as long as there aren't more than fifty! And your father's pălincă, as long as Gennaro doesn't drink it all.
And before you leave, I have to give you something.
A letter for Grandma Assunta. I wrote it in Neapolitan, so she can see I'm learning. Giulia helped me… a bit.
A bit? I rewrote it three times! But I'm glad you tried.
CHÉ = "keh" with a closed E and final stress: ben-KEH, per-KEH, pur-KEH.
Double FF and final stress: af-fin-KEH.
When you express a feeling about SOMEONE ELSE's action, you use the subjunctive:
Sono felice che tu sia venuta.
mi dispiace che, è un peccato che
mi stupisce che, è strano che
In Romanian we say "mă bucur că ai venit" (indicative), but in Italian it's the subjunctive: "sono contento che tu sia venuto".
For something that has already happened: subjunctive of AVERE / ESSERE + participle.
I think Gennaro drank all the pălincă.
Te lo dico perché tu lo sappia.
È uscito senza che nessuno lo vedesse.
"Anche se" (even if) takes the INDICATIVE: "Anche se piove, esco." Only "benché / sebbene" take the subjunctive.
Ti do la ricetta perché tu possa farla.
Tip: if you can replace it with "affinché", it's the subjunctive.
With the same subject, the conjunctions become prepositions + infinitive:
Although she's tired, Giulia is working.
I'll explain everything so you understand.
Let's leave before it gets dark.
I'll come, provided you drive slowly.
"Even if it rains, I'm going out."
"I'm staying at home because it's raining."
"Before I leave, I'll call you." (same subject)
Prima che io parto, ti chiamo.
Sono contento che tu sia venuto.
Although she doesn't speak Italian, she makes herself understood.
Di che cosa ha paura Matei?
Che sua madre si senta persa
Perché Matei e Giulia non vanno?
In che lingua ha scritto Matei la lettera?

At Naples airport Doina stopped in front of the sliding doors and took Ilinca's hand. "Mi-e frică," she said. Although she had raised two children and worked for forty years in a school, at that moment she looked like a child on her first day of school.

The doors opened. On the other side there was a crowd: Gennaro with an enormous sign ("WELCOME DOINA AND ILINCA" written in red, with two mistakes), Giulia's mother Rosaria with a bunch of flowers, three cousins, two aunts and, in the middle, sitting on a folding chair someone had brought from home, Grandma Assunta.
Assunta stood up slowly and opened her arms. Doina didn't understand a word she said, but she understood everything. They hugged in the middle of the airport, and nobody dared interrupt them.

The four days were a whirlwind. On Friday Rosaria taught Doina to make pastiera, even though they spoke different languages. They used gestures, eyes, hands covered in flour. "More wheat!" said Rosaria. "Mai mult zahăr!" answered Doina. Ilinca translated when she could, but soon realised there was no need.

On Saturday Doina made sarmale for twenty people in a Neapolitan kitchen the size of a handkerchief. Gennaro ate eleven. "Mamma mia," he said, patting his stomach. "I'm glad my sister is marrying a Romanian. As long as his mother comes to cook every Christmas."

On Saturday evening Gennaro took Doina and Ilinca to the seafront to see the bay. Doina stood silent for a long time in front of Vesuvius, the wind in her hair. Then she said in Romanian: "Now I understand why she misses the sea." Ilinca translated for Gennaro, who was moved, although he pretended he had something in his eye.

On Easter Day, after Mass, the whole family sat down at an extremely long table. Both cuisines were on the table: pastiera next to cozonac, sarmale next to casatiello, Gennaro's wine next to Ion's pălincă. Before they started eating, Assunta asked for silence. She took a letter out of her bag. "Matei wrote it," she announced. "In Neapolitan."

She read it aloud. It was full of mistakes, and at every mistake the cousins laughed. But at the end there was a sentence Matei had written on his own, without Giulia correcting it: "Grandma Assunta, I promise you that your granddaughter will be happy. Even if I speak badly, my heart speaks well."

Nobody laughed this time. Assunta folded the letter and put it in her bag, close to her heart. Then she looked at Doina and said something in Neapolitan. Ilinca translated, her voice trembling: "She says she's glad your son has grown up like this. And that she wants to meet the person who taught him to speak with his heart."
Doina smiled. Then she took Assunta's hand and placed it on her own chest. No translation was needed.

On Monday, at the airport, Doina's suitcase was heavier than when she'd arrived: inside were two pastiere, a casatiello, three bottles of limoncello and a recipe handwritten by Rosaria, in Italian, so that Giulia could translate it for her in Sibiu. And in her heart, a new ninety-one-year-old friend.
Come comunicavano Rosaria e Doina in cucina?
Con i gesti, gli occhi e le mani
Che cosa aveva scritto Matei alla fine della lettera?
«Anche se io parlo male, il mio cuore parla bene.»
